misconceptions.description: Believing that demographic parity, equalized odds, and calibration can all be satisfied simultaneously
misconceptions.trigger: learner promises a model that is 'fair on every metric'
misconceptions.feedback: When base rates differ, the impossibility theorem says these criteria cannot all hold at once. A defensible design surfaces the trade-off rather than denying it.

misconceptions.description: Conflating demographic parity (equal selection rates) with equalized odds (equal error rates)
misconceptions.trigger: learner uses one definition's language to satisfy the other
misconceptions.feedback: Demographic parity equates selection rates across groups. Equalized odds equates error rates given true labels. These are different measurements answering different ethical questions.

misconceptions.description: Picking a single fairness criterion regardless of deployment context or where harm lands
misconceptions.trigger: learner applies the same criterion across hiring, criminal risk, and medical triage
misconceptions.feedback: Match the criterion to where the concrete harm lands and which kind of error matters most in that context. Different contexts make different criteria the louder requirement.

misconceptions.description: Treating individual fairness as objectively defined without recognizing the role of the distance metric
misconceptions.trigger: learner cites individual fairness as the value-neutral fair criterion
misconceptions.feedback: Individual fairness's content depends on the distance metric d. Choosing d encodes which attributes count as 'similar' and which do not — itself an ethical choice that should be surfaced.
